--- title: "K-nearest neighbors" subtitle: "STA 363 | Meeting 4" author: "Dr. Lucy D'Agostino McGowan" footer: "[Dr. Lucy D'Agostino McGowan](https://lucymcgowan.com) | STA 363 | figures from *ISLP* (James, Witten, Hastie, Tibshirani and Taylor, 2023)" logo: "img/icon.png" format: revealjs: theme: [default, custom.scss] slide-number: c/t show-slide-number: all chalkboard: true menu: true preview-links: true code-overflow: wrap code-line-numbers: false highlight-style: github title-slide-attributes: data-color: "#d5008f" execute: echo: true warning: false message: false editor: source jupyter: python3 --- ## Outline ::: {.incremental} * The Bayes classifier * K-nearest neighbors * Flexibility as a tuning parameter ::: # The Bayes classifier {.center} ## The Bayes classifier ::: {.definition} Assign $x_0$ to the class $j$ with the largest $$\Pr(Y = j \mid X = x_0)$$ ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.question} Why can we never use this on real data? ::: ::: ## Bayes decision boundary ![](img/islp/fig2_13.png){fig-align="center" width="60%"} ::: {.source} ISLP Figure 2.13. One hundred observations in each of two classes. The purple dashed line is the Bayes decision boundary. The Bayes error rate is 0.133. ::: ## K-nearest neighbors ::: {.definition} To classify $x_0$, find the $K$ closest training points and take a vote. ::: ::: {.fragment} $$\Pr(Y = j \mid X = x_0) \approx \frac{1}{K}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{N}_0} I(y_i = j)$$ ::: ## KNN with $K = 3$ ![](img/islp/fig2_14.png){fig-align="center" width="70%"} ::: {.source} ISLP Figure 2.14. Left: the three nearest neighbors of a test point. Right: the resulting decision boundary. ::: ## KNN with $K = 10$ ![](img/islp/fig2_15.png){fig-align="center" width="58%"} ::: {.source} ISLP Figure 2.15. KNN with $K = 10$ in black against the Bayes boundary in purple. Test error is 0.1363 against a Bayes rate of 0.1304. ::: ## KNN with $K = 1$ and $K = 100$ ![](img/islp/fig2_16.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"} ::: {.source} ISLP Figure 2.16. The same data with $K = 1$ on the left and $K = 100$ on the right. ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.question} Which is high variance? Which is high bias? ::: ::: ## Training and test error ![](img/islp/fig2_17.png){fig-align="center" width="52%"} ::: {.source} ISLP Figure 2.17. KNN training error in blue and test error in orange as $1/K$ increases. The dashed line is the Bayes error rate. ::: # In Python {.center} ## The Default data {.small} ::: {#a6fffc15 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} DATA = "https://lucymcgowan.github.io/sta-363-f26/data/" Default = pd.read_csv(DATA + "Default.csv") Default.head(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {#43f0744a .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} Default["default"].value_counts(normalize=True).round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` default No 0.967 Yes 0.033 Name: proportion, dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## KNN in scikit-learn {.small} ::: {#6a839ab2 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline X = Default[["balance", "income"]] y = (Default["default"] == "Yes").astype(int) X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split( X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=363, stratify=y ) ks = [1, 3, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 200] train_err, test_err = [], [] for k in ks: m = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k)) m.fit(X_train, y_train) train_err.append(1 - m.score(X_train, y_train)) test_err.append(1 - m.score(X_test, y_test)) ``` ::: ## Error rate against 1/K {.small} ::: {#5e2485f5 .cell execution_count=5} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](04-knn_files/figure-revealjs/cell-6-output-1.png){fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.question} Why is training error at $K = 1$ guaranteed to be zero? ::: ::: ## Curse of dimensionality ::: {.incremental} * KNN works well when $p$ is small and $n$ is large * As $p$ grows, the nearest neighbors stop being near * With $p = 20$, capturing 10% of the data needs 80% of every range ::: ## Application exercise 4 ::: {.takeaway} Tuning $K$, and finding out what happens when you forget to scale. ::: ## Before Wednesday ::: {.nonincremental} * Read ISLP Sections 5.1.1 to 5.1.3 * Problem set 2 due today * Check-in 2 on Wednesday ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.question} We picked $K$ by looking at the test set. What is wrong with that? ::: :::
